/blog/offseason-25-robust-vision.title: Offseason `25 | Robust Vision - FRC Team 4788
p: One thing we identified we wanted to improve for for the 2026 season was our vision processing. We had numerous issues with both options we tried during the 2025 season but also parts we liked about both. We had issues with electrical robustness and the LimeLight software when using the LimeLight 4s, then again had issues with electrical robustness and packaging when using RPI5s running PhotonVision. To combat this for this year we are planning to use an X86 Mini PC running PhotonVision. Locking this in now has allowed us to develop a robust mounting approach and develop a custom regulator to power it. Running a minipc also provides us with a lot of flexibility with our vision in season, being able to change out our cameras very easily and add more software features if we need, as we have plenty of processing left over. Our case and regulator designs can be found below:

/blog/2024-build-blog-design-guidelines.title: 2024 Build Blog - Design Guidelines - FRC Team 4788
p: Inspired by Spectrum’s design guidelines we created our own. Our process was to run though Spectrum’s as a template, and steal the best and invent the rest. The “inventing the rest” for us looked like removing irrelevant guidelines or guidelines that didn’t reflect our own team limitations, and then adding any guidelines we have experienced. This is a process we have never previously documented before season, and only discussed.
Make a good robot (be in the meta)
Shoot during pick and place games
Pick up flat objects at a steep angle
Ramp bot (we expirenced this in 2018, in the end we removed our ramps and won the comp)
Corner mounting (One of our students made quite a good system last year, I think it was inspired by 8177 Vector)
Create standard for battery lead direction
Above bumper + 150 mm away from motors
Bushings for slow motion is ok
Remove control from driver to give control to robot
LED’s must also serve a purpose

/blog/offseason-25-carbon-fibre-shafts.title: Offseason '25 | Carbon Fibre Shafts - FRC Team 4788
p: In 2025 we utilised Carbon Fibre for the first time, both in static structure and as a replacement for hex shaft.We found some great benefits of doing this, however being our first time we also ran into multiple issues. The purpose of this blog post is to detail our solution to the problem of robust bearing support. This project was under taken by a collection of grade 9 students.

On our 2025 robot, we secured our CF shafts to our structure using HDPE bushings with aluminium runners. This was step one in weight reduction, removing the mass of a large heavy bearing. One issue we found with this, was that the increased friction generated heat which in some locations made the bushing bind. Other than that the function met or exceeded our expectation.
Our solution was utilising the following as KPIs:
No wear on the carbon fibre shaft after 30 minutes of use at a 5-10 degree angle for a 1kg weight/load (fail state)
It should be less than 20 grams so it is less or equal to a normal hex bearing
Our design had several undocumented iterations, but our final solution is a plug that is epoxied into a CF shaft, and a flanged bearing that is held in by a custom bearing hat.
Shipping not included, check link, need 1 but comes in 10
Will be made by techies (39.24 for 4m of round aluminium)
Get the F697ZZ 7X17X5 flange bearing, need 1 but comes in 10
it costs this much to make 1 thing

/blog/offseason-25-electrical-can-connec.title: Offseason `25 | Electrical CAN Connectors - FRC Team 4788
p: Going into the new season we identified that one area we wanted to improve on for our 2026 robots was our electrical robustness as we had multiple issues between competitions and during build season with electrical that slowed us down greatly.

One of these issues was an inability to quickly identify and diagnose CANBus issues as all connections were soldered, to fix this issue we will use 5 custom PCB designs to route both our RIO and CANivore CANBuses, as well as 12V and DIO lines (for RIO network only) over standard RJ45 (ethernet) cabling, allowing for quick disconnection and rerouting of CAN signals, whilst retaining a robust connection

The Rio Hub acts as a connection between the RoboRio's CANBus output and the RJ45 Bus that connects to it. The board also provides reverse polarity protection and voltage regulation (if the regulator is installed) for 12v supply, 4 DIO lines over RJ45 and 8 through Molex SL connectors, 2 PWM lines for servos over Molex SL connectors and the board mounts to the MXP port of a RoboRIO
The Rio modules act as nodes to connect one or more CAN devices to the network, they also provide DIO access and 12v output, they can be soldered to terminate the bus.
Functions similarly to the Rio Hub, without DIO lines, PWM or voltage regulation, has mounting holes that line up with the CANivore mounting holes
Functions similarly to the Rio Modules but without DIO access, it is compatible with Rio modules and Hubs, but won't pass through the DIO lines (to be fixed in the next iteration)
A simple 8V-22V to 12V regulator that can be plugged into the Rio Hub and held down with the mounting hole (not lined up correctly in current version)

/blog/2025-cad-resources.title: 2025 CAD Resources - FRC Team 4788
h1: Onshape Resources - Learning Course, FeatureScripts, and More
p: Team 4788 switched to Onshape from AutoDesk Inventor before the 2025 REEFSCAPE Season. Since then we have been building up resources to improve the learning and design processes.

We found the FRCDesign.org learning course a great resource for learning CAD, but the use of imperial measurements made it far less applicable for our team. Over the 2025-2026 preseason we began the mammoth task of adapting FRCDesign.org to metric. It is still a work in progress, but the course can be accessed at learn.team4788.com. We plan to add additional resources to this site in the future, such as a programming guide.
Over the preseason, we also developed some FeatureScripts to automate parts of our design process. These include:
Wire Channel - On the billet drive bases we built in 2025, we used channels cut into the underside of the drive base to route wires neatly. This FeatureScript automates the channel creation process.

Tube Converter - Based off the Tube Converter from Julia's FeatureScripts, this script serves a similar purpose of creating tubes with hole patterns, but simplifies the interface, makes it better suited for metric tubes, and adds a preset for WARES tube.

Spacer - This FeatureScript can create spacers for 1/2" hex shaft, 3/8" hex shaft, round shaft, or 8 mm keyed shafts, with options to engrave the spacer length. It is similar to the one in Julia's FeatureScripts but creates different style spacers and is better suited for metric.
The FeatureScripts can be found here. We plan to continue adding to them in the future.

Over the 2025 season and 2026 preseason we have also been putting together a part library, consisting of evergreen custom parts and configurable pulleys, fasteners, bearings and spacers. It also contains uploaded WARES parts and parts from other vendors not on MkCAD.
The part library can be accessed here. It will continue to be updated in the future.

/first.title: Team 4788
h2: FIRST® (For Inspiration and Recognition of Science and Technology) is a non-profit, international organization founded in 1989 by Dean Kamen, an inventor and entrepreneur. Its goal is to inspire and educate young people in the fields of science, technology, engineering, and math (STEM) through a mentor-based teaching system. ​
"To transform our culture by creating a world where science and technology are celebrated and where young people dream of becoming science and technology leaders."

FIRST® is comprised of multiple robotics programs, all aimed at different age groups. This includes the Lego® League Explore, FIRST Lego® League (FLL), FIRST Tech Challenge (FRC), and the flagship FIRST® Robotics Competition (FRC), in which 4788 Can't Control competes in. Each year, FIRST® releases a new game for each program. This game poses an enormous challenge composed of various tasks, and teams must strategize, design, prototype, build, program, and test their robot during build season, which lasts for six weeks. After build season, teams compete in numerous regional tournaments to qualify for world championships, held annually in Houston.

In FIRST® robotics, we value Gracious Professionalism® and Coopertition®. Gracious Professionalism, a term coined by FIRST® advisor Woodie Flowers, is the backbone of FIRST®, motivating innovation and respect for team members and competitors alike. With Gracious Professionalism, teams compete honorably but still treat one another with mutual kindness. Coopertition adds on to this by encouraging the notion that in the heat of competition, teams can help and learn from each other and other teams. .
More information about can be found at the FIRST® website, including details about Previous FRC Games.

/outreach.description: As the first FIRST team in our home of Western Australia, we pride ourselves on creating an inclusive and ever-expanding community of FIRST in WA.

/about.title: Team 4788
h2: We envision a Western Australia where every student, regardless of geography, identity, or socioeconomic background, has the opportunity to engage in meaningful STEM experiences. Through sustainable outreach, strong community, and student-led innovation, Team 4788 aims to grow a diverse and resilient robotics environment that inspires the next generation of problem-solvers and changemakers.

Our mission is to inspire students across Western Australia through world-class robotics, hands-on engineering, and inclusive STEM outreach. Team 4788 empowers young people, especially those in under-served communities, to build exceptional robots, grow as leaders, and pursue excellence.
p: Team 4788 - Can't Control is a FRC (FIRST Robotics Competition) Team, but we are more than robots. Based out of Curtin University, Perth Western Australia, we are an eclectic community of like-minded individuals who work together to Ignite, Improve, and Innovate.

Our team aims to improve our skills, technical and nontechnical, in a team environment supported by university students, staff, and industry professionals. We work in as a team similar to sports, to build an compete with robots! These robots weigh up to 60kg and can be as tall as 1.5m.
